articles.title: The Lindsay Clancy trial renewed focus on postpartum psychosis. What’s next?
articles.author: Barbara Rodriguez
articles.summary: The high-profile murder trial of Lindsay Clancy — which ended in a mistrial last week after a jury was unable to convict or acquit the Massachusetts mother in the 2023 strangling deaths of her three young children — put a renewed spotlight on postpartum psychosis, the severe psychiatric condition her lawyers say she was suffering from at the time. As attention moves on from the trial, some researchers want more concrete changes that could improve how postpartum psychosis is researched, treated and prevented. How that happens — and how quickly — is unclear. While some in the mental health community applaud the improvements in how postpartum psychosis is recognized, others think the condition needs a more formal diagnosis for better long-term research. But the overall medical consensus, researchers say, is that postpartum psychosis is treatable when diagnosed early, and that outcomes as severe as Clancy’s are incredibly rare. They hope the trial, which has spurred frank conversations online among mothers about the complexities of postpartum mood and anxiety disorders, can also lead to productive conversations between patients and doctors — instead of panic . articles.summary: I placed my panic-rations on the checkout counter: a carton of milk, three cans of Spaghetti-Os, and a sleeve of Oreos. Jet black U.S. fighter jets shot through the sky as military vehicles prowled empty streets. If this was the apocalypse, I was sure we were going to die. It was a strikingly beautiful morning, just beginning to feel like fall, as the sun came up on 9/11 in New York City. I’m still shocked at how quickly it all flipped into a nightmare. But 25 years later, I feel nostalgic for a time when devastating tragedy had the galvanizing effect of bringing people together. Still, what was once common sense now feels like wishful thinking. Having witnessed all kinds of New Yorkers helping total strangers without batting an eye on 9/12, 9/13, 9/14, and for years into the future, I found the immediate splintering of families and friends during the COVID-19 pandemic in Los Angeles an extraordinarily bitter pill to swallow. articles.summary: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. L ike most Americans, I spent September 11, 2001, filled with both rage and dread. I wanted the United States to find and kill whoever had planned this attack on my country. I knew little about al-Qaeda, but whoever did this, I thought, must pay. As the shock of that day wore off, I began to wonder, as so many others did in America and around the world, Now what?
